headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Napa County California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. Measure B in Napa County: Sales tax to fund wildfire prevention and open space preservation. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Napa County and additional election information, visit the Napa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. State Assembly District 12: Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward compete in a battle between business and labor. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Sonoma County and additional election information, visit the Sonoma County Registrar of Voters website. headlines.title: 2 San Jose police officers arrested, charged after internal investigation
headlines.description: Two San Jose police officers were arrested and charged with evidence tampering and filing a false police report, the department announced Thursday. Raydarius Surry, 29, and Destiney Thompson, 30, are accused of confiscating drugs from someone on the street to replace drug evidence that was lost in another case, according to police. The two are in a relationship and have been with the department for several years – eight for Surry and six for Thompson. Back in August, police launched an investigation into Surry in connection with an arrest he made on May 3. Surry was notified by the department in August that a small baggie containing a small amount of suspected narcotics, which had been listed in his police report, was never booked into evidence, according to police. The baggie was slated to be tested by the county crime lab. On Aug. 12, after being told about the missing evidence, Surry stopped a pedestrian unrelated to the May 3 case and found a similar baggie of suspected narcotics, police said. Surry seized the baggie, did not take any additional enforcement action and later booked the baggie into evidence under the May 3 case number. He did not document the Aug. 12 stop or evidence seizure. Police said Thompson watched body camera footage of the May 3 arrest to allegedly help Surry formulate a plan to replace the missing evidence. “When you take that careless mistake and you conspire to cover it up and plant evidence and create a false police report, now you’re talking about a felony and tremendous erosion of public trust in the department,” legal analyst Steven Clark said. Surry and Thompson surrendered late Wednesday evening and were booked into county jail, police said. They later posted bail and were no longer in custody as of Thursday evening. “Officers are required to maintain the chain of custody without exception and to be completely truthful in their accounts of interactions with the public,” San Jose police Chief Paul Joseph said in a statement. “Falsifying evidence or police reports is a crime, and our Department moved swiftly to remove both officers from duty and pursue criminal accountability. These allegations, if proven to be true, constitute a failure to live up to the standards our community has a right to expect. I will not tolerate any Department member violating the sacred trust placed in us.” Surry was placed on paid administrative leave on Sept. 2 while the investigation was underway, according to police. Thompson was placed on paid administrative leave on Sept. 18. Investigators are conducting a thorough review of both officers’ cases, arrests and evidence bookings, the department said. No other discrepancies have been found so far. Silicon Valley De-Bug, a police watchdog group, said the case impacts the department’s credibility. “This is affirming to those that have said that police are not infallible and that they do lie and that they do make up evidence, they plant evidence,” Silicon Valley De-Bug organizer Raj Jayadev said. In a statement, the San Jose Police Officers’ Association said it was deeply disappointed, writing, “If proven true, their actions run counter to the level of honesty and integrity necessary to wear our uniform. The POA will not fund their legal defense…” SJPD referred the case to the California Commission on Peace Officer Standards and Training for temporary decertification review, police said. The police department’s Criminal Investigations Detail referred the criminal investigation to the Santa Clara County District Attorney’s Office, which filed charges Wednesday afternoon.

headlines.title: Family of boy with autism wins countersuit against neighbor in San Jose
headlines.description: A neighbor sued a San Jose family whose son has autism, claiming the child’s grunts in the back were a “nuisance.” The family countersued and, this week, a jury ruled in their favor. Ezequiel, known as Zeke, is a 14-year-old teenager who suffers from Level 3 autism, a severe form of the disorder that sometimes involves loud grunting. “It requires very high support needs. Usually full care with dressing, bathing, toileting, dangers, safety. It’s a lot,” Zeke’s mom Serena Arvayo said. Zeke and his mom lived with her dad in a home in San Jose until a neighbor filed a lawsuit, claiming her property value was dropping because of Zeke, and that she was suffering emotional distress, labeling the child a “nuisance”. That’s a word the family says traumatized them. “It was hurtful. You use that for an animal, or a car alarm that won’t shut off. But not an autistic individual,” Arvayo said. “Completely outrageous. I mean, how can a family intentionally inflict emotional distress on a neighbor because the child was innocently playing in the back yard and making noise? Sounds of joy,” Elizabeth Hansen with Behar Gibbs Savage Paulson, LLP said. Arvayo says it took away Zeke’s humanity. They moved out of her dad’s rental home, so as not to cause more problems, but the neighbor’s lawsuit remained in place. Arvayo then countersued and both suits went to trial. “It’s a challenge. We can’t just live anywhere. An apartment, we won’t live in. Sharing walls is very difficult because we’re always very careful and mindful of other people, but I always now go next door and say ‘Hey, this is my son. If you have any worries, please come talk to me’,” Arvayo said. This week, the Arvayo family won the countersuit. The same jury awarded them $8 million. Arvayo says it gave her son his humanity back. “My son was represented with dignity. And that was the most important thing for him, to have the dignity he deserves,” Arvayo said. “I think the jury in this case was sending a message. That in a civilized society, we need to have empathy and compassion, and civility at its most basic level,” Arvayo’s lawyer Missy Cornejo said. “This delivers a message to people think they can get away with bad behavior. You better be careful because you might pay the consequences,” Arvayo’s lawyer Ron Rossi said. Repeated messages to the plaintiff’s lawyer have not been returned. The Arvayo family now is relieved, hoping Zeke has given other children on the spectrum a voice.

headlines.title: Having kids out of the question for many Bay Area residents due to high cost of living
headlines.description: The cost of living in the Bay Area is keeping many couples from starting a family, according to a recent survey. Of the roughly 1,800 childless adults younger than 50 surveyed by Joint Venture Silicon Valley, with the Bay Area News Group, 56% said they are unlikely to have children and 58% said they can’t afford to raise kids in the Bay Area. “The screaming headline is that people feel hammered in the Bay Area,” Joint Venture Silicon Valley President and CEO Russell Hancock said. “They can’t afford to live here, and it’s getting worse. The main thing that’s upsetting to folks is that housing seems like it’s now completely out of reach.” NBC Bay Area’s Christie Smith has more in the video report above.

headlines.title: Dream defeat Valkyries to force decisive Game 7 in WNBA Finals
headlines.description: Allisha Gray scored 23 points and Rhyne Howard had 21 as the hot-shooting Atlanta Dream held off Golden State’s late rally to take an 80-69 victory over the Valkyries in Game 6 on Thursday to pull even in the WNBA Finals. The decisive Game 7 will be played at Golden State on Saturday night as each team seeks its first WNBA championship. After having their lowest scoring games of the Finals in losses in Games 4 and 5, the Dream enjoyed an offensive awakening when faced with the must-win mandate. On Wednesday, the Dream announced a sellout for Game 6 despite the much-criticized 12:30 p.m. ET tipoff. There were only scattered empty seats in the upper level despite concerns about work and school obligations hurting the turnout. Angel Reese recorded a double-double with 15 points and 13 rebounds for Atlanta. Gabby Williams led the Valkyries with 26 points. Tiffany Hayes added 15. Valkyries Playoffs 9 hours ago Golden State Valkyries 11 hours ago Atlanta’s biggest lead was 25 points. The Valkyries stormed back in the final minutes, pulling to 77-66 on Laeticia Amihere’s two free throws with 1:57 remaining. After being held to 22 points in the first half of their 65-55 loss in Game 5, the Dream matched that total in the first 6:30 of the opening quarter. Much of the production came on 3s. Atlanta made 6 of 8 3s and 11 of 15 shots overall while racing to a 32-15 lead in the first quarter. After leading 6-5, the Dream pulled away with 13 unanswered points in a run that included two 3s from Jordin Canada. Reese joined the 3-point party with a shot from the corner in the second period. Entering the game, the Dream were 15-0 when Reese had at least one 3. While Atlanta’s sharp shooting continued for a 46-26 halftime lead, the Valkyries struggled. Golden State made only 9 of 34 shots in the half, often struggling to create open opportunities because of the Dream’s smothering defense. Howard opened the second half with another 3-pointer. Valkyries guard Veronica Burton was called for a flagrant foul later midway through the third period when an officials’ review determined she made an unnecessary windup and contact on Howard’s face as Howard was driving for a basket. Kaila Charles closed the third quarter with a 3-pointer for Golden State that trimmed Atlanta’s lead to 16 points at 63-47. It was the smallest lead for the Dream since the 13-0 run in the opening period. Golden State pulled to within 13 points at 68-55 before Gray and Reese sank 3s to push the lead to 74-55. Williams’ three-point play cut the led to 77-69 before Gray sank a crucial 3-pointer for Atlanta. Hayes was called for her fifth foul in a collision for a loose ball with 5:01 remaining. Hayes left the court slowly after receiving attention from a trainer.

headlines.title: Young girls skip school with their parents to attend Valkyries' early WNBA Finals watch party
headlines.description: Sika Lopez took 11-year-old daughter Kendra out of school Thursday to be part of the early morning watch party outside Chase Center cheering for the Golden State Valkyries. Lopez grew up in Los Angeles watching Lisa Leslie and the Sparks, and believes being present can impact Kendra chasing her own dreams — so they joined several thousand fans gathering on the plaza at Thrive City outside Chase Center to support Golden State in Game 6 of the WNBA Finals at Atlanta. “This is such a monumental moment. The Valkyries have worked so hard. When I was her age this wasn’t even possible,” Sika said between clapping along with the others. “Lisa Leslie growing up, she was larger than life.” The Valkyries lost 80-69 as Atlanta forced a winner-take-all Game 7 back in the Bay Area on Saturday. It will be the first seventh game in WNBA Finals history, and one team will capture its first championship. The loss hardly kept Golden State fans from celebrating what this means for women’s basketball in the Bay Area and far beyond. Wendy Franklin-Willis and longtime friend Liz Shaw couldn’t wait for one more. “She played hooky for this,” Shaw said of Franklin-Willis, a middle school teacher in the East Bay suburb of Castro Valley. “I love the community and we’re behind the Valkyries. No matter what happens.” Added Franklin-Willis: “They’ve already won by getting here, a second-year expansion team, no real superstar, such the way the game should be played, and here they are, a game away.” WNBA 11 hours ago Valkyries Playoffs 9 hours ago “This is incredible,” Franklin-Willis said. “You have two teams, Atlanta’s been to the final but has never won, you have two teams with young players. You have the misfit, poised Valkyries against Atlanta, yeah, amazing.” Earlier, hundreds of hands raised when energetic in-arena host Ari Waller asked if fans had taken a day off work or school to attend the violet-clad watch party, where fans received rally towels upon entry and Violet the beloved raven “bestie” — no, she’s not a mascot — danced and posed for photos. Kendra Lopez missed a day of sixth grade in the East Bay to root on the Valkyries and her favorite player, Kayla Thornton. “It makes a big difference because the Valkyries are such a young team and to be able to support them so early means something to me,” Kendra said. Joshua Padilla from Santa Clara felt the same way, bringing his two daughters to San Francisco — 15-year-old high school sophomore Mariah and 10-year-old Malia, who is in fifth grade. Both girls told their teachers they had doctor appointments, along the lines of what point guard Veronica Burton had suggested when she noted after Game 5, “Call in sick, I recommend it.” “It’s just really special. I’m happy to be here with my sister and my dad, we never really get the quality time,” Mariah said. “I think this is a great way, something we all connect with and we love the Valkyries.” Despite the early hour and some frustrated supporters about the scrutinized early tipoff time at 9:30 a.m. PDT, “Ballhalla” braved commuter traffic to be in place for this event and watch the game on the big screen, which is 74 feet wide and 42 feet high. Though the Valkyries trailed 46-26 at halftime, being part of this memorable scene meant far more than the score in a game that finished before lunch time on the West Coast. For Padilla, he knows how important it is to expose his daughters to powerful, athletic women not to mention all of the diversity in the Valkyries’ fan base. They considered it a great day no matter who won. “That’s exactly why I wanted to have them come out here, women’s sports is thriving right now and it’s becoming bigger,” he said. “I actually have four daughters, so being able to come with two of them and support the women and women’s sports it just shows them that it’s up and coming and there’s something to strive for later on down the road.” ___ See AP’s full WNBA coverage here

headlines.title: How NASA Ames' lunar landing simulator helps prepare for moon missions
headlines.description: The United States is going back to the moon. Part of the training goes through the Bay Area, where the NASA Ames Research Center has a lunar landing simulator. The simulator is a system of motors, hydraulics and technology that serves as a crucial testing platform. It allows pilots and astronauts to simulate a landing on the moon, as well as a boat or shuttle launch or another kind of spacecraft. Astronauts have used the platform before countless expeditions into space. NBC Bay Area’s Scott Budman got the chance to strap in on Thursday and give it a ride. Watch his full report in the video above.

headlines.title: Former Oakland city employees testify in Sheng Thao corruption trial
headlines.description: Former Oakland city employees took the stand on Thursday in the Sheng Thao federal corruption trial. Latonda Simmons, Oakland’s former assistant city administrator, testified that former Mayor Sheng Thao asked her to become city administrator if she won the mayor’s race. Simmons said she was disappointed when Thao appointed Harold Duffy interim city administrator. Simmons said she also felt excluded from homelessness discussions during the time of the alleged corruption scheme. Defense attorneys questioned Simmons’ motives for testifying, pointing to her grievances with Thao and other city employees. Simmons acknowledged doing her own investigation after the feds searched Thao’s house, and sharing research with prosecutors on what she believed was a broader conspiracy. Sheng Thao Oct 28 Sheng Thao Oct 27 Sheng Thao Oct 26 Sheng Thao Oct 23 Former city administrator Jestin Johnson also took the stand and testified about a meeting with businessmen David Duong and Mario Juarez. Johnson said Thao and her chief of staff asked him to meet with the Duongs about their recycling company, California Waste Solutions. But he testified the discussion turned to modular housing through Duong’s other company, Evolutionary Homes, including a proposal by the businessmen to bypass the normal city contract approval process. Johnson said the units were too expensive and stressed any homeless housing solutions contract would require a competitive proposal process open to other companies. On cross-examination, he acknowledged Thao often asked him to meet with community members and business owners. Prosecutors allege Thao and her boyfriend, Andre Jones, conspired with the Duongs to help get her elected mayor in exchange for granting them city contracts and a commitment to buy the housing units. The government’s key witness Mario Juarez is expected to take the stand on Friday for his highly anticipated testimony. Juarez, deemed a co-conspirator by prosecutors, previously pleaded guilty in the case.

headlines.title: Doordash to acquire Instacart for $17 billion, creating delivery giant
headlines.description: Delivery giant DoorDash is buying to-your-door grocery service Instacart for $17 billion, the company announced Thursday. The deal means users will be able to order groceries and items from other retailers via DoorDash and its delivery network. The companies said Instacart customers can now shop at more than 50,000 additional stores on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today. DashPass and Instacart+ members will now also pay one membership fee instead of two. DoorDash is expected to keep the Instacart brand and its technology. Until the transaction closes, DoorDash and Instacart will continue to operate as separate and independent companies. “Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more,” said Chris Rogers, CEO of Instacart. DoorDash shares gained more than 9% in pre-market trading Thursday. The deal represents the latest chapter of consolidation in the delivery industry. Last year, DoorDash bought UK-based Deliveroo, while Uber now owns Postmates ​and Delivery Hero. DoorDash has emerged as the most successful stand-alone online delivery platform in America, commanding some two-thirds of all food-delivery volumes as of 2024, according to Bloomberg data. But over the past year, the company has seen its share price decline by approximately a third, largely due to rising costs. Instacart, meanwhile, reached the pinnacle of its success during the Covid-19 pandemic, when lockdowns sent millions of consumers to their phones to order up groceries. But the company’s stock has gone nowhere over the past two years, as Instacart struggled to find new paths to growth while facing increasing competition from Amazon and Walmart’s grocery-delivery offerings. While a merger would create cost-savings by allowing the combined company to reduce its corporate workforce and split some expenses, it’s not clear how much more money there remains that can be squeezed out of delivery customers. Americans who eat at home have begun to complain about the price of food delivery — and the pinch has only worsened this year amid soaring fuel costs, which have led to new fees and surcharges. A recent debate about the cost of having a burrito delivered went viral, as social media users argued over whether $20 was a reasonable price to pay to have the Tex-Mex treat delivered. Platforms like DoorDash and Instacart have also faced legal scrutiny over how they treat workers who deliver for their respective platforms. Last month, DoorDash settled with New York City regulators for $131.5 million to resolve charges it deprived workers of millions of dollars in tips. “Simply put, we screwed up,” the San ‌Francisco-based ⁠company said in a statement. “Our mistakes meant some Dashers were underpaid or paid late. While these mistakes weren’t intentional, that doesn’t make them okay.” The proposed transaction was first reported by tech website The Information and The Wall Street Journal.

headlines.title: Google-parent Alphabet's stock price plunges, erasing more than $500 billion in value
headlines.description: Shares of Google parent company Alphabet sank on Thursday by as much as 15.8%, putting the company on course for its worst single-day drop in history. The plunge also instantly wiped out more than $550 billion in market capitalization, also ranking as the company’s worst one day market value loss ever. It also ranks as the second-worst wipeout in market history, only behind Nvidia’s $589 billion drop in 2025. Google is still America’s fourth largest company by market value, and its shares are worth more than $3.4 trillion, all told. But the sharp drop in its stock price Thursday was the latest sign of a broader anxiety creeping through Wall Street over how long it will take big artificial intelligence companies to see consistent returns on their massive investments. The significant selling came after the company reported its latest quarterly financials Wednesday, revealing that revenues fell short of Wall Street expectations. It also reported lackluster advertising sales. The “magnitude” of the slowdown in Google’s search business was “steeper than expected,” JPMorgan Chase analysts wrote in a Thursday morning note. A senior Alphabet executive told investors Wednesday that part of the reason ad revenues from search were underperforming was because of Google’s own “AI Mode” search feature, which was resulting in fewer ads. The company is working on addressing this, senior vice president Philipp Schindler said on the investor call, adding that “ad experiments” in the feature have “shown promising results” Company executives tried to soften the blow for investors by touting more than 1 billion users of its Gemini AI app. But all that AI is coming at a massive cost to Alphabet, which disclosed that it has committed to more than $1 trillion worth of multi-year spending agreements to fund the infrastructure, energy and leases required to run AI systems. The company said during its July earnings report that it planned to spend more than $200 billion this year, which is double what it spent in 2025. The company in June also raised almost $80 billion in capital, also to spend on the ever-expanding AI buildout. Alphabet’s disappointing results also came against the backdrop of better results from its peer Microsoft, whose shares initially rose in after market trading Wednesday and overnight, beforereversing course to fall about 2% by 10:50 a.m. ET Thursday. The big drop in Alphabet shares dragged down the Nasdaq Composite index, which was down 1.6% by mid-morning. The S&P 500 fell slightly less, by about 0.6%. Stock in the chip companies that supply equipment for AI data centers followed Alphabet shares lower, with the Philadelphia semiconductor index dropping 1.6%. The bleeding even spread beyond the tech sector, as shares of construction equipment giant Caterpillar — a key supplier of the machines required to build data centers — plunged 9% early Thursday. Caterpillar’s recent earnings report revealed that the company’s revenues beat Wall Street expectations, but by less than many traders had hoped. As investors clamor for ever-higher returns from companies linked to the costly AI buildout, stock in firms that only narrowly top earnings targets, like Caterpillar, have been punished with dramatic sell-offs.

headlines.title: Worker rights pioneer Dolores Huerta wanted others to feel seen
headlines.description: Dolores Huerta had spent decades advocating for labor rights and marginalized people when she went to a central California college and met a group of farmworkers’ descendants — many of them students who choked back tears over the then-94-year-old taking the time to listen to them. That was the effect Huerta had on young people, said Ana Padilla, executive director of the Community and Labor Center at the University of California, Merced, which had hosted Huerta for the event. “It was transformative,” Padilla said. “Something that I heard a lot from students in particular was just how accessible she was. That’s just what made Dolores a natural organizer, just an ability to connect immediately with really anyone.” The activist and icon who helped improve the lives of laborers in farming and other industries died Wednesday from cancer at 96. She was surrounded by family at her home in Bakersfield, California. While most people would spend their golden years enjoying retirement, Huerta never stopped fighting. Living up to her famous rallying cry, “Sí, se puede!” (“Yes, it can be done”), the civil rights activist marched alongside protesters, spoke on countless panels and lent her voice to progressive causes well into her 90s. And it wasn’t just on issues impacting Latinos but also African Americans, the LGBTQ+ community and women. Not just an organizer, Huerta during every major election encouraged voters and endorsed candidates. She also pushed more Latinos to consider running for office. Even after Huerta revealed in March that she was among the women and girls who say they were sexually abused by César Chavez, the labor leader she was inextricably linked to in history, admiration for her only strengthened. Huerta once said she simply wanted to encourage younger generations, particularly women, to use their voice. “I hope that they know they have a place,” Huerta told The Associated Press in August while attending the Los Angeles premiere of the documentary, “American Pachuco.” “Never be afraid to take the leadership,” she said. Civil Rights Oct 28 In Memoriam Oct 28 A living Latina legend who continued to show up From the United Farm Workers union to the Latino Victory Project, many groups said they would not exist if not for Huerta. She co-founded with Chavez the National Farm Workers Association in 1962. It would become the United Farm Workers of America a few years later and then join with the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee. The movement fought for better wages and working conditions for agricultural workers such as fair hours and access to bathrooms. Her work has garnered her accolades including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2012. Her leadership has made Huerta almost a mythical figure, especially in Latino households. Anabelle Sanchez, 20, of Lansing, Michigan, texted her parents when she learned of Huerta’s death. Sanchez, who is Mexican American, was a child when her mother taught her about Huerta. “I’ve always looked up to her. She was very civically involved throughout her life and just using her voice even when things were scary,” said Sanchez, a Michigan State University political science and public policy major who hopes to emulate Huerta’s “strength and her courage.” “She was a part of everyday life and she would always go to events like pretty much up until her last breath,” Sanchez said. “Always being an advocate, thinking of others who may not have that opportunity. That’s just something that will always stay with me about her.” Irasema Coronado, director of Arizona State University’s School of Transborder Studies, became friends with Huerta over 20 years ago when they met at a feminist-centered conference on a cruise ship. She remembers Huerta as someone with boundless energy who showed up for people. She recalls Huerta attending a protest in Phoenix and then leaving immediately after to make appearances at demonstrations in New Mexico and Texas. “She was everywhere,” Coronado said. “She never missed an opportunity to be on the right side of something. I never saw her with a script. It was from the heart.” An unapologetic feminist During the farmworkers movement of the 1960s, Huerta put up with a great deal of sexism being the only woman in the room. “She was expected to be quiet and stay in the background and instead, she was out in front and demanding change,” said Kathy Spillar, executive director of the Feminist Majority Foundation, of which Huerta served on the board. The two women met at a conference for the National Organization for Women in the late 1980s. Spillar approached Huerta with the idea of launching the foundation. “It was the only way that the issues Dolores was talking about could be addressed,” Spillar said. “She said, ‘Sign me up. I’m with you.’ And that was the beginning of almost 40 years.” Spillar met Huerta around the time that a police officer attacked and beat Huerta. On Sept. 14, 1988, while protesting outside an appearance by then-Republican presidential candidate George H.W. Bush in San Francisco, she was beaten with a baton. Huerta was hospitalized with broken ribs, a ruptured spleen and other injuries. She later won an $825,000 settlement from the city. But, that ordeal also got Huerta thinking about how to help others besides farmworkers, Spillar recalls. Huerta noticed the women caring for her at the hospital as she recovered from the police assault were under-appreciated. “They all would talk with her about the struggles that they faced,” Spillar said. “And she decided, I think then, that she was going to become very active in the feminist movement.” A larger-than-life figure who connected with people Many schools in California bear the name Dolores Huerta. The state also joins Washington, Oregon and New Mexico in marking her legacy on her April 10 birthday. However, after the revelations about Chavez’s abuse, Huerta rejected pledges by some to use her name as a replacement for his on streets, schools and other sites. Instead, those places “should not be renamed after her, but the UFW martyrs, organizers, farmworkers, and families who sacrificed everything to build something bigger than any one person,” a spokesperson for Huerta told The San Francisco Standard earlier this year. Huerta used her influence when it felt needed. That’s how the labor center in Merced was officially founded in 2020, Padilla said, after the labor rights pioneer lobbied state lawmakers to fund it. Talking to students there was among Huerta’s favorite things. “She would want to spend as much time as she could with you and regardless of your standing,” Padilla said. “She treated folks the same.” ___ Associated Press writers Leslie Ambriz in Los Angeles and Fabianna Rincon in New York contributed to this report.

headlines.title: Motorcyclist killed in crash on westbound I-80 in Fairfield
headlines.description: A motorcyclist was killed early Thursday morning in a crash that shut down an on-ramp to Interstate 80 in Fairfield, according to the California Highway Patrol. At 4:22 a.m., officers were alerted to a report of a motorcycle crash on the Manuel Campos Parkway on-ramp to westbound I-80. Five minutes later, they found the 37-year-old male rider at the scene, unconscious. “The Fairfield Fire Department arrived shortly after and immediately initiated life-saving measures. Tragically, despite the exhaustive efforts of first responders, the rider succumbed to his injuries and was pronounced deceased at 4:36 a.m.,” the CHP’s Solano-area office said on social media. Authorities shut down the on-ramp. It was reopened around 6 a.m., the CHP said. The CHP said that the rider, driving a BMW sportbike, was entering westbound I-80 from Manuel Campos Parkway. But due to his speed, the rider failed to properly traverse the curve on the on-ramp and crashed. “The officers and staff of CHP Solano extend our deepest condolences to the family, friends, and everyone affected by this heartbreaking incident,” the agency said. The motorcyclist’s identity will be released by the Solano County Coroner’s Office after his next of kin has been notified of his death. Anyone with information regarding this crash is asked to contact the CHP’s Solano-area office.
